opus-5.5.text:
Hugging Face is fantastic. It has made models accessible to everyone, and that's a huge contribution to the community. But from the perspective of our research on learning from populations of neural networks, what we call model zoos and weight space learning, it has some real limitations.

The biggest one is that the models there aren't generated in a controlled way. Different people upload them for different purposes, with different architectures, training procedures, datasets, hyperparameters and preprocessing. Often the metadata is incomplete: you don't know exactly how a model was trained, what data it saw, or how it was evaluated. As a source of individual models to use downstream, that's fine. But if you want to treat models as data points and learn something systematic about the weight space, it's a problem.

To learn from weights, you need structure in the population. You want to vary one factor, like the seed, the initialization, the learning rate or the dataset, while keeping everything else fixed. That way you can attribute what you observe in the weights to specific causes. On Hugging Face you have a very heterogeneous, long-tailed collection. There are a few very popular base models and then lots of fine-tuned variants, and they aren't sampled in any principled way. So there's a lot of confounding.

There's also the question of training dynamics. Usually you only get the final checkpoint, maybe a few intermediate ones. For us, the trajectory through weight space during training is extremely informative. Seeing how models evolve, where they diverge, when they start to generalize or overfit, all of that is mostly missing.

That's why we've invested in building our own model zoos: large, systematically generated populations of models with documented training settings and checkpoints across training. Hugging Face complements that nicely as a "model zoo in the wild," and over time it becomes interesting to test whether what we learn on controlled zoos transfers to those real-world populations. But on its own, it isn't a clean dataset for weight space learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Hugging Face is wonderful, right? It's this huge repository, hundreds of thousands of models, and for our work on model zoos, on populations of neural networks, you'd think it's the perfect data source. But the problem is that it's essentially a convenience sample. People upload what they happen to have trained, and there's very little structure to it.

So you have models with the same architecture, say a ResNet or a BERT variant, but you have no real idea how they were trained. The hyperparameters are often missing, the seed is missing, the data is sometimes described, sometimes not, the number of epochs, the optimizer, the learning rate schedule, all of that is frequently just absent from the model card. And many of those models are not trained from scratch at all, they're fine-tuned from the same handful of base checkpoints, so what looks like diversity is really a few lineages with small perturbations on top.

For what we want to do, which is to treat the weights themselves as a data modality and learn something about how training conditions shape the weight space, that's a serious limitation. You can't do controlled analysis if you don't know what varied between two models. You can't ask, how does the learning rate show up in the weights, if you don't know the learning rate. So Hugging Face gives you scale but not control, and that's exactly why we ended up generating our own model zoos, where we systematically vary the factors we care about, keep everything else fixed, and know the full provenance of every single model in the population. It's smaller, but you can actually do science with it.

astra-6.text: The limitation is that Hugging Face gives you access to a huge number of models, but finding the right one for your task is still difficult. A model’s description or benchmark score doesn’t necessarily tell you how it will behave on your data. So access to models is only part of the problem; we also need ways to compare them and understand which ones are useful for a particular application.

sol-6.1.text: Hugging Face is a fantastic resource, but the limitation is that you mostly get the final model. You don’t necessarily know exactly which data it was trained on, how it was trained, or how it relates to other models beyond what’s documented in the model card. And that documentation varies quite a bit. So if you want to systematically compare models or understand why their behavior differs, having access to the weights alone isn’t enough.
